summary: Describes how Sieve email filtering, with some extensions, can create automatic replies based on the recipient's address book and presence information. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A mail helper that answers for you, replying one way to friends and another way to strangers, depending on whether you are around.

questions: how to create intelligent email auto-replies
subtitle: Using email filtering rules to send smart automatic replies based on presence and address book.

tldr.problem: Email systems need to send automatic replies to incoming messages, but naive auto-responders send too many useless responses or reveal private information.
tldr.mechanism: Sieve email filtering, combined with presence information extensions and address book lookups, enables rules that reply only to known senders, vary the reply based on the recipient's availability status, and avoid excessive or inappropriate responses.
tldr.outcome: Administrators and users can create intelligent auto-responders that respect privacy, avoid mail loops, and adapt to the recipient's presence. Smart filtering helps manage information overload.

facts.label: Presence states supported
facts.value: away, do not disturb, busy, extended away

today: RFC 6133 is an Informational RFC describing how to use Sieve with extensions to create presence-aware auto-responders. All the referenced extensions have been published as standards. Sieve is widely deployed in enterprise email systems and some consumer platforms. The guidelines in this RFC help implementors and users create auto-responders responsibly, reducing mail loops and unwanted disclosures while automating legitimate notification scenarios.

sections.title: Intelligent Email Automation
sections.content:
This document describes how the Sieve email filtering language, combined with several extensions, creates automatic replies to incoming email. Sieve, defined in RFC 5228, allows email systems to execute scripts that filter and process messages. Traditional auto-responders are blunt tools: they send the same response to every sender or subject.

The Sieve approach enables intelligent responses. Auto-replies can be conditional: a recipient's personal assistant receives detailed availability information, family members receive one message, colleagues receive another, and unknown senders may receive nothing. The system can check the recipient's presence status (away, do not disturb, busy, extended away) before deciding whether to send a reply. Different presence states can trigger different responses. The mechanism automatically tracks previous replies to the same sender, avoiding mail loops and excessive messages.

Users should nevertheless be thoughtful about auto-replies. Email is not instant messaging; senders expect replies to take time. Over-use of auto-replies contributes to information overload.
sections.eli5: Email systems can run programs that automatically reply to messages you receive. These programs can check who the sender is, what you said you were doing, and send different replies to different people.

sections.title: How Intelligent Auto-Replies Work
sections.content:
A Sieve script checks several pieces of information about each incoming email to decide whether to send an auto-reply. The Notify extension (RFC 5435) provides the notify_method_capability action, which queries the recipient's presence information. The Notify-Presence extension (RFC 6132) extends this with specific presence states such as away, do not disturb, and extended away.

The External-Lists extension (RFC 6134) allows the script to look up the sender's address in the recipient's address book or other contact lists. The script can group contacts (family, friends, colleagues, customers) and apply different rules to each group.

The Vacation extension (RFC 5230) provides the vacation action, which sends an automatic reply message. It automatically avoids sending multiple replies to the same sender within a specified interval. The Vacation-Seconds extension (RFC 6131) allows intervals as small as zero seconds, supporting high-frequency auto-responses such as service request acknowledgments.

The Variables extension (RFC 5229) allows scripts to extract values (such as the recipient's presence status message) and use them in replies.
sections.eli5: The script can ask 'who is this from?', 'is this person in my address book?', 'am I away right now?', and then send different replies based on the answers.

sections.title: Use Cases for Presence-Based Replies
sections.content:
The RFC provides five detailed examples. In Example 1, the script replies only to senders in the recipient's default address book and only when the recipient's presence shows extended away status. The reply includes the recipient's own presence message extracted from the presence system. Replies are limited to one per sender every 30 minutes using the Vacation-Seconds extension.

In Example 2, the personal assistant receives detailed information about the recipient's status depending on whether they are away, do not disturb, busy, or extended away. Family and friends receive a general unavailability message. Others receive nothing, preventing information leaks to unknown senders.

In Example 3, the script checks the sender's address book list and presence status to send replies only to work colleagues during extended absence, including alternative contact information.

In Example 4, the script acknowledges every incoming message from non-staff addresses with zero-second intervals, implementing a request acknowledgment system.

In Example 5, the script forwards copies of certain messages to a backup person based on sender lists and subject line urgency, using the redirect action rather than vacation replies.
sections.eli5: The examples show different ways to use the rules: reply to friends but not strangers, send different messages to your boss than to family, acknowledge customer requests automatically, or forward important messages to a backup person.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
Auto-responders introduce several security and privacy concerns. Excessive messages can result from script errors, potentially creating mail loops or overwhelming senders. With minimal reply intervals, errors become more severe.

Information disclosure is a major risk. If the script logic checks the wrong address book list or omits list checks entirely, private or confidential information can be sent to inappropriate recipients. Example 3 demonstrates this: detailed business trip information should only reach colleagues, not arbitrary senders.

Presence probing is a subtle attack. A sender who recognizes that replies depend on presence status can send multiple messages and observe whether replies are sent, inferring the recipient's actual presence without authorization. This creates an unintended back door into presence information.

Covert channels emerge when senders can detect changes in auto-reply behavior, allowing a recipient to signal information by changing presence status or script configuration.

An auto-responder can also leak cryptographic material. Timing attacks on cryptographic operations in the script could leak key information. If the script returns results of decryption operations, an attacker can use chosen ciphertext attacks to compromise encryption keys.

Authors of Sieve scripts must carefully consider what information they expose and to whom, and implementors should warn users about over-using auto-replies.
sections.eli5: Mistakes in the script can send private information to the wrong people. Attackers can send you messages to figure out if you are actually away. Bad scripts can accidentally leak secrets. Users should think carefully before creating auto-replies.
